sentences.text: Lucianovenator is an extinct coelophysoid theropod dinosaur distinguished by a unique combination of four specific pairs of paired pits on its cervical vertebrae.

Its anterior cervical ribs are exceptionally long, measuring more than five times the length of the vertebrae, while the edge of each lamina develops a deep pit that grows progressively longer toward the base of the neck.
The animal possesses anterior cervical ribs that are exceptionally long, measuring more than five times the length of the cervical vertebrae.
It features a unique autapomorphy where the edge of each centrodiapophyseal lamina develops a long, deep pit that grows progressively longer and deeper toward the base of the neck.
The genus name Lucianovenator means "Luciano's hunter" and honors Don Luciano Leyes, who first reported the fossil remains discovered in 2014 by paleontologist Ricardo N. Martínez and his team.

The holotype specimen PVSJ 906 was found in the Quebrada del Puma locality within the Quebrada del Barro Formation in Argentina and consists of an articulated sequence of vertebrae from the third cervical to the fourth dorsal, along with a sacrum and a partial pelvis.
Three additional specimens consisting mainly of sacra and partial pelves, plus a proximal right tibia tentatively attributed to the species, have also been referred to Lucianovenator.
The genus Lucianovenator was formally named by Martinez and Apaldetti in 2017.
Lucianovenator is one of the few known neotheropod dinosaurs from South America.

An initial phylogenetic analysis placed Lucianovenator in the family Coelophysidae alongside Coelophysis rhodesiensis and Camposaurus, but later phylogenetic studies recovered it as a coelophysoid that is not a member of the Coelophysidae family.
Fossils date to the late Norian to Rhaetian stages, approximately 210 to 202 million years ago, though other estimates place the Norian stage between 227.3 and 205.7 million years ago.
